extracted.intended_audience: EPA rulewriters, regulated power plant owners/operators, environmental regulators, and stakeholders/commenters on CAA section 111 NSPS/BSER for electric generating units
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and procedural standards used by the EPA to determine whether carbon capture and sequestration (CCS) is the Best System of Emission Reduction (BSER) for coal-fired steam generating units, including which sources are affected, whether CCS is adequately demonstrated, and whether costs and resources make it reasonable to require CCS. Covers technical performance, cost metrics, workforce and materials availability, legal constraints, and modeling assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affected sources capacity estimate (42 GW long-term)
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of the BSER analysis, EPA considers that 42 GW of coal-fired generating capacity will be operating by 2039 and therefore constitutes the affected sources in the long-term subcategory that would be subject to requirements based on CCS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This determination is based on multiple lines of analysis including announced retirements, historical trends, and model projections; EPA does not claim precision as to which units will remain but treats the two sets of sources as reasonably representative for BSER analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unit age analysis to project retirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze the fleet by unit age: from 2000 to 2022 the average age of a unit that retired was 53 years; the present average age of operating fleet is 45 years; of 81 GW not announcing retirement/conversion, 56 GW will be 53 years or older by 2039.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use age-based projections (e.g., assume retirement at average retirement age) to estimate capacity remaining; EPA provides example calculations showing amounts older than 53 by 2032 and 2039 and uses these to infer likely retirements/exemptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical retirement rate (rate-of-change) analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Use historical average annual coal retirements (8 GW/year from 2009-2023) to project future fleet size (projecting at that pace yields 45 GW by 2039).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA also presents an alternative projection assuming units retire at age 53 (resulting in 38 GW by 2039) and treats these approaches as reasonable bounds for expected remaining capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of unannounced/late-announced retirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that many coal units announce retirement only a few years in advance; e.g., of 15 GW reporting 2022 retirement, only 0.5 GW had announced in 2017.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on currently announced retirement dates; account for the empirical tendency of late announcements when estimating affected source population.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of baseline modeling (IPM) to estimate economic retirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate modeling baseline projections (e.g., IPM) which project additional retirements due to economic reasons (IPM baseline projected 42 GW operating by 2039 and that 39 GW of the 81 GW without announced retirements will retire by 2039).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine modeling outputs with historical/announcement data to inform the representative inventory of sources for BSER without requiring exact unit-level prediction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distance to sequestration site and exemption timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider distance of units to potential saline sequestration sites and the interaction with a finalized exemption for sources permanently ceasing operation by January 1, 2032; units far from storage (>100 km or >160 km) may be more likely to retire before applicability dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA provides percentages and GW amounts for units beyond 100 km and 160 km that will be >53 years old in 2032/2039 to justify possible exemptions based on likely retirement due to age.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resources and workforce sufficiency requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate that sufficient resources and an available workforce exist (or can be trained) to install and operate CCS at the necessary scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA relies on DOE order-of-magnitude assessments of specialized equipment and commodity materials, commodity production comparisons, large supplier pools for specialized equipment, and workforce estimates showing available transferrable skills and apprenticeship programs; quantitative job estimates and comparisons to existing construction workforce provided as supporting evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commodity/materials supply adequacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether commodity materials (e.g., steel, cement, MEA solvent, TEG) and specialized equipment (absorbers, strippers, heat exchangers, compressors) are available at required scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DOE analysis found maximum annual commodity requirements much lower than global production for most commodities; MEA could be ~14-24% of global annual production in scenarios, but steel and cement requirements are an order of magnitude lower than U.S. annual production; specialized equipment supply bottlenecks are unlikely due to large supplier pool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workforce availability and transferability
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate workforce needs (construction, engineering, manufacturing, electrical/plumbing/mechanical trades) and the ability to train/expand via existing programs and apprenticeship systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Majority (~90%) of direct jobs expected in construction (project-based); DOE/other estimates of jobs per plant and aggregate job projections provided; compare required jobs to existing industry construction employment to show adequacy and availability of transferable skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequately demonstrated technology legal standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A technology is 'adequately demonstrated' if there is sufficient evidence that the EPA may reasonably conclude a source applying the technology will be able to achieve the associated standard of performance under the reasonably expected operating circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The standard allows reliance on commercial-scale data from individual sources and on identified technological improvements; the technology does not need to be in widespread use at promulgation, but implementation at necessary scale in a reasonable period must be supportable by evidence and precedent (text, context, legislative history, judicial precedent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable timeframe for deployment
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must determine that demonstrated technology can be implemented at the necessary scale in a reasonable period of time, recognizing installation requires building capture facilities, pipelines, and sequestration sites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA cites D.C. Circuit caselaw supporting allowance of time for installation and notes that nothing in comments changed their view of appropriate deployment timing; this factor interacts with subcategory cutoff dates (e.g., Jan 1, 2039 and Jan 1, 2032 exemptions).

rubrics_metrics.name: CCS performance level considered adequately demonstrated (90% capture)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA concludes that CCS technology with 90 percent capture is adequately demonstrated for coal-fired steam generating units and that the 90 percent standard is achievable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA bases the determination on available data from commercial-scale sources and relevant analyses; specific citations support achievability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on reliance on EPAct05-assisted projects
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory provisions in EPAct05 preclude EPA from relying solely on experience of facilities that received EPAct05 assistance but do not preclude reliance on such facilities in conjunction with other information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA follows its 2015 NSPS interpretation: may use EPAct05-assisted project experience as part of the evidence package, but not as the sole basis for adequacy demonstration; commenters' criticisms were addressed in RTC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost reasonableness metrics ($/MWh and $/ton CO2e)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA assesses cost reasonableness using increase in cost of electricity ($/MWh) and control cost per ton removed ($/ton CO2e), comparing to historical benchmarks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA cites benchmarks of ~$18.50/MWh (FGD retrofit range) and ~$98/ton CO2e (conversion from a prior methane rule), treating them as useful indicators but not bright-line standards; aggregate and per-ton/-MWh measures, industry revenues, capital expenditures, and price effects are also considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumptions for cost assessment: capacity factor and amortization
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA assumes an 80% annual capacity factor (NETL default 85% cited) and evaluates multiple amortization periods (12-year baseline, 8-year, 7-year) to calculate $/ton and $/MWh costs for CCS retrofits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example results: 12-year amortization & 80% capacity factor → −$5/ton CO2 reduced (−$4/MWh); 8-year → $19/ton ($18/MWh); 7-year → $29/ton ($28/MWh). EPA treats fleet averages and notes substantial capacity can install CCS at reasonable cost even with 7-year amortization for many units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of IRC section 45Q tax credit in cost-to-source
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA takes into account the IRC section 45Q tax credit (assumed $85/metric ton when prevailing wage/apprenticeship requirements are met) because it reduces the cost of controls to the source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA reasons the tax credit is part of the cost of controls to the source, is available to all sources installing CCS, may be monetized/ transferred, can be carried back/forward, and legislative history indicates Congress anticipated EPA would consider the tax credit when evaluating CCS costs. If prevailing wage/apprenticeship requirements are not met, the credit value falls to $17/metric ton; EPA assumes investors will meet requirements to maximize $85 value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of 45Q on utilization assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume sources installing CCS will increase utilization (operate at higher capacity factors) due to economic incentives provided by the 45Q tax credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modeling projects units with CCS run at ~80% or higher capacity; NETL baseline assumes 85% default for coal CCS retrofits; EPA cites analogous behavior of wind projects receiving production tax credits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capture plant and CO2 transport & sequestration cost modeling assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Cost analysis assumes one CO2 capture plant per coal-fired EGU and a single common CO2 pipeline for multi-EGU plants; transport and storage costs are calculated to the nearest saline reservoir using models (e.g., NETL CO2 Transport Cost Model).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NETL estimates include pipeline capital, related capital expenditures, O&M; sequestration costs include site screening/evaluation, permitting/construction, injection wells/equipment, operation/maintenance, pore volume acquisition, long-term liability protection, and regulatory compliance costs (UIC Class VI, GHGRP subpart RR); main sequestration cost drivers are injection rate and areal extent of CO2 plume (dependent on reservoir thickness/permeability and sequestration coefficient).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of IIJA and IRA infrastructure and program effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for Federal programs under IIJA and IRA that are expected to increase CO2 pipeline infrastructure, develop sequestration sites, and otherwise reduce costs (e.g., Carbon Dioxide Transportation Infrastructure Finance program, Regional Direct Air Capture Hubs, CarbonSAFE, extension/increase of 45Q).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA treats these statutory programs as likely to result in further cost reductions and infrastructure development that support deployment and reduce transport/sequestration costs, especially for new combined cycle EGUs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison to prior control costs and administrative precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare CCS costs to costs of other emission controls previously required (FGD for SO2, SCR for NOX) and to costs from GHG controls in other industries to assess reasonableness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA uses prior rule cost equations and historic capacity factor assumptions to generate benchmark $/MWh ranges (e.g., wet FGD $14.80–$18.50/MWh; SCR $10.60–$11.80/MWh) and compares per-ton metrics to prior GHG rule findings (e.g., $98/ton CO2e from methane rule). These comparisons are indicative, not determinative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of revenue offsets from byproducts (EOR, recovered gas, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that revenues from utilization or sale of byproducts (e.g., CO2 for EOR, recovered gas) can reduce control costs, but EPA's treatment varies by rule and it may choose not to account for such revenues in determining BSER.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA cited prior instances where it considered recovered-product revenues in cost calculations (e.g., methane recovered/sold, electricity from landfill gas) and noted in 2015 NSPS it recognized but did not account for EOR revenues when determining BSER.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reevaluation against prior CCS conclusions (CPP and ACE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Revisit prior determinations that CCS was not BSER (CPP and ACE) in light of reduced CCS costs and increased tax incentives (45Q) reflected in updated NETL reports and IRA provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA explicitly identifies cost reductions and 45Q extension/increase as key developments warranting reevaluation; cites updated NETL reports (most recently 2022) showing lower costs relative to 2015 inputs.
